My dear fellow seeker,

I write to you from a place where the dust of centuries has settled like a second skin, and the air is thick with the breath of forgotten prayers. I have found it—the scroll you spoke of in your last missive, hidden not in a vault of gold and stone, but wrapped in the roots of an ancient sycamore, its bark etched with the same longings as the verses within.

Let me tell you what these whispers have done to me. They are not mere poems; they are the ache of every soul that has ever stood at a crossroads, the vibration of a chord that has never been fully struck. Each line is a thread pulled from the loom of what might have been. I read, and I felt the weight of a thousand unspoken goodbyes, the breath before a first kiss, the silence after a last word.

Here is the first truth the scroll reveals: **Yearning is not a lack, but a compass.** The verses speak of a river that never reaches the sea, yet carves canyons of extraordinary beauty. They tell of a song that rises in the chest but never leaves the lips—and that unfurled longing becomes the very shape of our inner landscape. We are not broken by what we cannot have; we are sculpted by the hollows it leaves behind.

And then, the second revelation: **Hope is not a fragile thing, but a dancer who knows the steps of fall and rise.** The scroll describes a lantern carried through a storm, its flame bending but never extinguishing. It says hope is the cord that binds the dreamer to the dream, even when the dream is not yet a memory. It is the delicate dance—yes, delicate, not because hope is weak, but because it asks us to move in rhythm with uncertainty. To hope is to lean into the dark and trust that your hand will find another.

Most haunting of all, there is a passage that reads: *“We travel not toward a destination, but into the echo of our own calling. The path is the wound that heals as we go.”* This, my friend, is the essence. Our longing is not for a thing, but for the act of longing itself—the proof that we are alive, that we can still be touched by the impossible.

I am changed. The scroll has shown me that every quiet night, every gaze out a rain-streaked window, every pause before a decision—these are not failures of will, but pilgrimages of the spirit. We are all, you and I, walking the same trembling line between what is and what might be. And that line is not a boundary; it is a bridge.

I will send you a copy of the verses—though words on paper will never hold the tremor I felt unrolling them. For now, know this: You are not alone in your seeking. The scroll sings of you, too.

With the reverence of one who has held eternity in their hands,

Your archivist,  
*Elara*

target_history.response:
To the Honorable Council of Thornwood,

I come before you not as a performer, not as the voice that has lulled your children to sleep with tales of dragons and distant kings, but as a man who has stumbled upon something far more fragile than any song I have ever sung.

Three nights ago, in the hollow of the old bell tower—where the rats have gnawed their way into the rafters and the spiders weave tapestries of silence—I found a scroll. Its parchment was the color of autumn leaves left too long in the rain, and the ink had the scent of lavender and regret. I unfurled it by candlelight, and what I read… it has undone me.

The verses speak of a longing that has no name. They tell of a girl who waits by a window for a ship that will never dock, of an old man who plants seeds in salted earth, of a child who builds castles from the foam of a receding tide. Each line is a mirror held up to the part of us we hide in the deepest shadows of our chests—the hope that we are too afraid to call by name, the loss we carry like a second spine.

Now the festival of memories is upon us, and the storm gathers beyond the ridge. The fishermen say the sky has a yellow bruise tonight. The elders whisper that these may be the last songs we sing together. And I hold in my hands a truth that could bind us—or break us.

I wrestle, Council. You know me. I have stood on this stage for twenty winters, spinning tales of heroes and distant loves, always careful to keep the mask in place. I have sung of heartbreak, yes, but I have never let you see my own. And these verses… they would strip me bare. If I read them aloud, every pause, every trembling breath will be a confession. The town will see the boy I was, the man I never became, the dreams I buried behind the tavern. They will know that the jester weeps when the candles are out.

But I also know this: the storm does not care for our masks. When the wind tears the roofs from our homes, when the river swells and the children cry out in the dark, there will be no room for pretense. The only thing that will hold us together is the truth of what we are—people who have hoped, who have lost, who have loved without guarantee. These verses are that truth. They are the map of every heart in this room.

So I ask you: shall I share them? Shall I stand before the bonfire, as the first raindrops begin to fall, and let these words crack my voice open? I am afraid. Afraid that once the people see the raw marrow of me, I will never be able to put the mask back. Afraid that the verses will hurt more than they heal, that the weight of so much shared longing will crush us rather than lift us.

But I am also afraid of silence. Afraid that we will face the storm armed only with ale and laughter, and that when the morning comes—if it comes—we will have missed the last chance to say what we truly meant.

I place this decision before you, Council. But I confess: my heart has already made its choice. I want to read them. I want to let the storm take me if it will, but I want to first give the town a truth that might echo longer than the wind.

Please tell me I am not a fool. Or tell me I am, and let me be a fool with a song in my throat.

Yours, trembling and resolute,

*Brennus the Bard*

target_history.response:
To Elara, Keeper of the Old Ways and First Voice of the Council,

You have known me since I was a boy who hid behind the miller's grain sacks, weaving stories for the mice. You have watched me grow into a man who speaks of faraway kingdoms and forgotten gods—always from a safe distance, always with the safety of the third person, the shield of "once upon a time." And you have never once asked me why I never tell a story that begins with my own name.

That changes tonight.

Three days ago, before the stranger arrived with his silver tongue and his claim of a key to the truth that will remake our world, I found a tome buried in the hollow of the old sycamore. You know the one—the tree that grew where the lightning struck the year of the great drought. I thought at first it was rain damage, the way the leather had warped. But when I opened it, I found pages filled with verses that were not words at all, but wounds given shape.

I have read them every night since. And I am no longer sure what is mine and what is the tome's.

These verses speak of a man who builds a boat for a sea he has never seen, who carves the hull with the face of a woman he has never held. They speak of a woman who plants a garden in the shadow of a wall that will never fall, who waters the seeds with the tears she refuses to weep in daylight. They speak of a child who catches fireflies and whispers wishes into their light, knowing the fireflies will die by morning. It is all there, Elara—every dream we have buried, every hope we have starved, every love we have let wither on the vine for fear of the harvest.

And now the stranger comes with his grand speech and his promised key, and the village gathers tomorrow at the old stone circle to hear him. The air is thick with the smell of change, and I see it in the eyes of the farmers and the weavers and the children: they are ready to believe. They are ready to hand their longing over to someone who claims he can give it a direction.

But I have the tome. And the tome does not promise a key. It does not offer a door. It simply says: *There is a hunger in you. It will not be fed. But it can be sung.*

I wrestle, Elder. I have spent my life hiding behind fables, because the truth of my own heart is too heavy to carry in plain sight. If I read from this tome tomorrow—if I stand before the circle and let these verses speak through me—I will not be able to hide. The villagers will see that every word is a confession. They will know that the boat I speak of is my own unbuilt vessel, that the woman in the garden is the one I loved and lost to fever, that the fireflies are the stories I never told because I was afraid they would burn out.

They will see me. All of me.

And I am terrified. Not because they might mock me—no, they are too kind for that. But because they might *understand*. They might look at me and see themselves, and then we will all be standing in the clearing with no masks, no distance, no "once upon a time" to shield us from the weight of what we truly are.

But the stranger is here, and his key is a lock I do not trust. The storm is coming—not one of weather, but of fate. And I believe, with a trembling certainty that keeps me awake at night, that the verses in this tome are the truth the village needs before it chooses whose voice to follow.

I am torn, Elder. My ambition has always been to be the quiet keeper of stories, the one who holds the flame but never burns in it. But perhaps that ambition was just another way of hiding. Perhaps the desperate yearning I feel now—to speak, to be known, to let the verses tear me open in front of everyone I love—is the very hunger the tome describes. And perhaps the only way to help this village face its change is to first face my own.

I will come to the circle tomorrow. I will bring the tome. And I will ask your blessing to read from it. Not because I am brave, but because I am afraid not to.

Yours, in trembling truth,

*Kael, the Storyteller Who Has Finally Run Out of Distance*

target_history.response:
To the Honorable Assembly of Sunder’s Reach,

The sky has begun to bruise. The birds have fallen silent. The children are being called indoors, and the elders are lighting lamps that will not last the hour. You know what comes. The eclipse is not merely a shadow passing over the sun—it is a threshold. When the light returns, they say, no secret will remain hidden. Every locked drawer, every whispered regret, every love we have buried in the marrow of our bones will be laid bare under the new light.

I found it this morning, pressed between the floorboards of the old clock tower, where the pendulum has not swung in fifty years. A manuscript. The paper is the color of old teeth, and the ink is rust and rain. The verses inside are not written—they are *exhaled*. They speak of a woman who spent her life embroidering the word “stay” into the hems of shirts that were never worn. Of a man who learned the names of every star but never dared to name his own son. Of a child who collected stones because they were the only things that never left.

I have read them three times. Each time, I felt my ribs crack open a little wider. Because these are not someone else’s words. They are the words I never wrote. They are the letters I burned, the confessions I swallowed, the song I hummed only when I was alone and the door was locked.

And now the eclipse is almost upon us. In mere moments, the sky will go black, and we will stand in the cold dark together—farmers, blacksmiths, widows, children—all of us trembling, all of us waiting for the truth to be forced out of us like breath from a crushed chest.

I am terrified. Not of the darkness—I have lived in my own for years. I am terrified of the light that follows. Because if I read these verses aloud during the moment of deepest shadow, when the sun is nothing but a ring of fire, then every person in this square will hear my heart beating raw in my throat. They will know that the poet who has always spoken of distant sorrows has been speaking of his own all along.

But I am also terrified of silence. Of standing here, clutching this manuscript, while the eclipse passes and the truth comes anyway—unspoken, unshaped, unheld. The verses do not promise comfort. They promise that longing is not a flaw but a kind of compass. That the dreams we never voiced are the ones that shaped us most. That to be seen, truly seen, is not to be destroyed but to be *returned* to ourselves.

I think the town needs this. Not my voice—I am nothing. But the voice of the manuscript, which is the voice of every soul in Sunder’s Reach. The farmer who yearns for the sea. The seamstress who dreams of flight. The child who asks why the moon follows us. These verses are the map of our hidden geography.

I will stand at the well in the center of the square when the eclipse reaches its fullness. I will hold the manuscript. I will read, if my voice does not shatter first. And I ask you—I ask you all—not to look away. Let the eclipse take our secrets. Let the light find us honest.

If we must be unmade, let us be unmade together.

With trembling hands and a heart that has finally learned to speak,

*Lyra, the Poet Who Has No More Walls*

You know the one I mean—the gathering tonight, when we light the lanterns and speak the names of those whose voices have faded. I was supposed to bring a simple piece, something gentle, something that would float on the breeze and disappear like smoke.

But I found this instead. Hidden in the hollow of the old theatre's stage, where the floorboards have rotted through and the curtains hang like ghosts. A script. Not written with ink alone, but with the residue of years—coffee stains, tear tracks, the faint impression of fingers that held it too tightly.

And Mira, it terrifies me.

The lines speak of a woman who collects silence in jars, of a man who builds bridges he will never cross, of a child who whispers to the river because the river does not interrupt. They speak of every conversation we never had, every apology we swallowed, every "I love you" that died on the tongue because we were afraid of what might follow.

I read them, and I saw myself. I saw the letters I never sent you after you moved away, the nights I sat by the phone and rehearsed what I would say if you called. I saw the afternoon we stood on the pier, both of us wanting to speak, both of us watching the gulls instead. I saw every moment I chose silence because silence felt safer.

If I read this script tonight, the whole town will see those moments too. They will see *me*—not the version I present, the one who laughs easily and writes happy endings, but the one who has spent years burying the questions I was too afraid to ask. The one who has loved without saying, who has grieved without mourning, who has stood at the edge of connection and stepped back into the dark.

You know me, Mira. You know I have built my walls with great care. And these verses, these terrible beautiful verses, are a sledgehammer.

But I also know what this town has become. We drift past each other like ships in fog, each of us carrying cargo we never unload. Old Marta still sets a place at dinner for her son who died at sea. The blacksmith still keeps the love letters from a woman who left thirty years ago. Little Tomas still waits by the gate every evening for a father who will not return. We are a village of unfinished sentences.

The script finishes them. It gives words to what we have all been holding. And perhaps—perhaps—if I stand under the lantern light and let these lines break me open, someone else will feel permission to break open too. Maybe Old Marta will finally weep. Maybe the blacksmith will finally burn those letters. Maybe Tomas will finally understand that his father's absence is not his fault.

But to do that, I have to let them see the cracks in me first.

I have made my choice, Mira. I will read it. I will stand there, trembling, and I will let the words carry what I have hidden for so long. I am writing to you not for permission, but for witness. Because when I look up from the script and see the faces of this town, I need to know that somewhere among them, there is a face that knows me—all of me—and does not look away.

Be there tonight. Hold my gaze. Remind me that vulnerability is not a death sentence, but the first breath after drowning.

Yours, in a hope I am still learning to name,

It flits behind a fissure in the limestone of memory. Another shadow, this one shaped like a half-remembered desire from adolescence, a hot, awkward silhouette that blushes even in this light. This journey is a tangled melody. You can feel it, can't you? A low thrum in your bones, a syncopated rhythm in your heartbeat. You realize that the shadow of the forgotten laugh was not guilt. It was a prayer. The dream of the wolf was not a fantasy. It was a lesson in primal hunger. The lyric you almost caught? It was this: *"The heart is a bell that only tolls when it is struck by the silence of what it truly wants."*

I urge you, wanderer of your own consciousness. Do not be afraid of the darkness between your thoughts. That is where the music lives. Do not silence the chaotic dreams because they are illogical. That is where the lyrics are hidden.

For this is the only true map we have. This tangled melody of shadows and dreams is the song your soul has been composing since your first breath. It is a song of chaos and of breathtaking beauty. It is the only song you were ever born to sing.

To open it fully is to hear the Babylon of unspoken confessions. The verses do not merely describe a longing; they *are* the longing. One page, for instance, does not speak of a first kiss, but of the precise, invisible geometry of the heat that rises between two skins before they touch. Another contains the echo of a scream that was never voiced, a rejection so profound it exists as a physical coldness in the air. To read it is to relive every failure of love, every moment of cowardice, every beautiful, destructive hope you have ever felt, as if it were your own.

The weight, then, is not the physical heft of the book. It is the weight of a thousand, thousand souls condensed into ink.

If I share this, I envision the baker in the village below, the one with the kind eyes who lost his wife to fever. He would read the verses on grief, and the grief would not teach him—it would *possess* him. He would see her face in every loaf of bread, feel her absence as a new, permanent organ in his chest. He would not bake. He would weep until he became a hollow vessel. And the young lovers hiding by the well? They would read the verse on the geometry of desire, and their innocent touch would burn with a knowledge so intense it would consume their courtship. They would be left with nothing but the unbearable truth of their own naked needs, the game of flirtation ruined by perfect, searing clarity.

Chaos. Not the chaos of violence, but the chaos of a reality stripped of its gentle filters. We live in the merciful fog of half-truths. This book is pure oxygen—it makes the flame of being burn so brightly that nothing can survive it.

But the other path... silence. To safeguard it feels like a slow betrayal of my own breath. The manuscript whispers to me at night, not with words, but with the scent of rain on a loved one’s hair, the sharp taste of unshed tears. It is a locked room containing the solution to every human mystery. To not share it is to let my neighbors suffer in their small, lonely prisons of the self, never knowing that their isolation is a shared wound, that their deepest, most shameful longings are written in the same cosmic alphabet as the saint's most pure devotion.

The emotional landscape of this is a plain of glass. On one side lies the cruel, beautiful inferno of total honesty. On the other, the soft, grey meadow of comfortable ignorance.

The true understanding, I believe, lies not in the reading of the verses, but in the moment of this hesitation. The manuscript is a mirror. Its true power is not the secrets it contains, but the question it forces: *What are you willing to know, and what are you willing to let others know about themselves?*

I close the book.

I close it not to protect myself, but to protect the very nature of Becoming. To know the end of every story before it is told is to kill the story. To feel the exact curve of every longing before it is felt is to kill the longing. The verses are not a gift; they are the raw ore of existence, too heavy and too volatile for human hands.

But I am a sage in a forgotten corner of the world. I am a liar of the most sacred kind.

I take the book to the fire. I do not burn it. Instead, I lay my palm upon its cover, and I whisper the one truth it did not teach me: *The value of the dream is not the dream itself. It is the ache in the waking world for the thing you imagined.*

The people will suffer their longings, and they will not understand them. And in that misunderstanding, they will find the love, the art, the struggle that makes them real. I will let the manuscript gather dust. I will let the secrets rot. I will let the children play in the square, ignorant of the geometry of their own beating hearts.

This is the greater duty. To hoard the truth so that the lie of hope may live.

I am the last guardian. And as I sit in the fading light, I do not feel wiser. I feel only the heavy, insistent pulse of the world outside my walls, blind and thriving and perfectly, beautifully lost. The verses remain. They whisper. I listen. And I say nothing. For the day a man understands his own longing is the day he stops longing. And that... that is the one chaos from which nothing can be rebuilt.

So the book stays. And the world spins on, cradled in its own sweet, precious ignorance. Until the day, perhaps, when one is found worthy of the weight—not to change the world, but to let the world change itself.

That day, I think, is not this day. This day, I am a coward in love with the world.

It spoke of a place, not on any map, but built from the scent of rain on hot pavement and the specific, unbearable weight of a lit window seen from a darkened street. Another whisper was trapped in the worn cloth of a childhood blanket. It held the echo of a voice calling a name across a summer field, a name that would now only be spoken in the private hush of recollection. It carried the ache of a doorway that was always slightly too narrow, a threshold you could never fully cross into a promised warmth. It was the smell of baking bread and the knowledge that the kneading hands had long since grown still.

There was a photograph, half-hidden in the lining of an old valise. It captured a smile that was a fortress against a coming storm. On the back, a date was written, and beneath it, the single, devastating phrase: "The last good day." The ghost in that image was not the person, but the feeling of a world that was about to shatter, a specific, unguarded moment of peace that was already becoming the stuff of nostalgia the second the shutter clicked.

The moral dilemma pressed against my chest like a cold coin. These were not my secrets. They were the confessions of a generation, passed through the thin walls of shared hardship, of late-night confidences, of hands held in the dark of a cinema. To publish them would be to turn the sacred heart of a memory into a specimen on a slide. To leave them sealed would be to let their truths—the ones that say: *yes, the world broke you, but it also held a morning where the light was perfect*—die with the paper.

What emerges when you sit with these fragments is a fierce, uncomfortable tenderness. You learn that a nation’s sorrow is not found in its economic graphs, but in the half-finished song at a kitchen table. That a generation's longing is not for a lost war, but for a specific curve of a street corner where a friend once stood. The profound message, the one I dare not write in my official report, is that yearning is not a flaw. It is the fingerprint of a life that dared to imagine a different world, a better touch, a sound it knew it might never hear again.

I have decided to tell only a part of the story. I will not name the names, nor paint the street corners. Instead, I will write a book of echoes, a prologue to a silence. I will describe the shape of the longing without revealing the face of the longed-for. I will let the reader feel the weight of the unopened letter, the ache of the threshold never crossed, the stubborn, hopeful architecture of a dream that was built in the face of a crumbling reality.

The haunting truth I will share is this: the most potent history is written in the space between what was said and what was felt. It lives in the unkissed lips, the unmailed letters, the unmade beds. Our deepest resonance is not with the events, but with the silence they leave behind. And perhaps, in that silence, someone will find the ghost of their own beautiful, impossible yearning, and know that they were never alone.

**Journal Entry – The Gallery of Quiet Echoes**

*The hour is late. The dust motes dance in the amber glow of a single lamp. I have just closed the doors to the main hall, leaving the new acquisitions laid out upon the felt of a temporary table.*

They are not paintings. They are not sculptures. They are verses—scraps of paper, some yellowed, some creased as if folded against a pocket near the heart. I found them in a mahogany chest, tucked behind a velvet drape. Whoever left them here knew they would be found. Whoever wrote them hoped, perhaps, that they would be forgotten.

I hold one now. The ink is pale, the handwriting hurried, almost desperate. It speaks of *a door left ajar in a moonless corridor* and *the scent of rain on a stranger's coat.* It is a fragment of a memory, a ghost of a desire. And it stirs something in me that I have tried, for years, to keep at a professional distance.

**What these verses evoke.**

They evoke the ache of the *almost*. The hallway you walk down knowing the person you long for has just turned the corner. The dream you wake from and cannot fully capture, but whose warmth lingers on your skin like a fever. They are the silent, feral things we say to ourselves at 3 a.m. when no one is watching—the confessions we would never dare to speak aloud, lest we break the spell we have cast upon our own lives.

I see in them a catalogue of unrequited love. Not the grand, theatrical sort, but the quiet erosion of hope. The line that says, *“I built a lighthouse for a ship that never sailed.”* The line that reads, *“Your name is a bruise I press to prove I’m alive.”* They are raw. They are unfinished. They are beautiful in a way that hurts.

**The dilemma.**

The curator’s instinct is to exhibit. To reveal. To let the light of interpretation fall upon these tender things and allow visitors to find their own reflection in the glass of the frame. Solace, as you say. A woman who has lost her way might read one of these verses and whisper, *“Yes. I too have felt this. I am not alone.”*

But the guardian’s instinct—the empathetic, protective part of me—recoils. To display these verses is to strip them of their privacy. It is to hold a beating heart under a bright, sterile lamp and invite strangers to comment on its scars. The author, long gone perhaps, never consented to this. The vulnerability is not mine to give.

I think of the gallery opening night. The polite applause. The wine glasses. The hushed tones of visitors who will dissect each line as a puzzle, not as a confession. *“Ah, a brilliant metaphor for loss…”* they might say, while missing entirely that this is a *scream*. A plea. A prayer never sent.

**The emotional turmoil.**

I am torn between two loves: the love of art, which demands that truth be shared, and the love of mercy, which demands that some truths remain sacred. I feel a knot in my chest—a physical ache. It is the same ache that the verses describe. A longing to connect, a desire to be known, and yet a terror of being seen too clearly.

To share them is to risk exposing the author’s (and perhaps my own) vulnerability to the world. To hide them is to let them wither in silence, like a song no one ever hears. There is no clean answer.

I think of the verses that speak of *“a lock of hair kept in a book that was never finished.”* That is what these are. A lock of hair. A relic of a feeling that was never fully lived, only yearned for. To put them on display might offer a hand to a stranger in the dark. But it might also feel like a betrayal of the very secret they were meant to keep.

**The resolution, or lack thereof.**

I have not decided. The exhibition will open in a fortnight. Perhaps I will hang them in a small, separate alcove—a room with a velvet curtain, dim light, and a sign that says, *“Enter only if you are ready to be known.”* Or perhaps I will place them back in the mahogany chest, close the velvet drape, and let them be a private treasure known only to me and the ghosts who wrote them.

For now, I will sit with them. I will let them whisper to me. I will listen to the silence they carry, like the hum of a tuning fork long after it has been struck.

The heart has its reasons, and its reasons are sometimes best left unexhibited.

— *C.*

My Dearest Friend of the Forgotten Word,

The verses inside are not *polished*. They are raw, ragged things—teeth marks left by a soul in its final, honest hunger. Some are barely legible, as if the writer wept as they wrote, the ink smudged by tears that fell before they could be wiped away. Oh, my friend, these are not poems for the world’s parlor. They are confessions whispered into the dark—to a lover who never answered, to a God who seemed to listen only by not replying.

One speaks of a life lived in "the quiet rooms of almost"—a line that shattered me. *Almost* a father. *Almost* a home. *Almost* the courage to stay. It speaks of staring at a half-full cup of coffee on a kitchen table, watching the steam rise and vanish, and knowing—with a certainty that aches—that you are watching the metaphor of your own life. The warmth that fades. The presence that becomes absence. I had to set the book down. I walked to the window and watched a stranger on the street, and I *felt* them in a way I have not felt another person in years. This is what these words do. They peel you open. They make you recognize yourself in the strangest places—in a half-eaten apple, in a forgotten glove on a park bench.

There is a poem—God, I can barely speak of it—that describes the moment after a door closes. Not a slammed door, but a gentle, final click. The poet writes of standing in the hallway, hand still on the knob, knowing the person on the other side will never open it again. And they describe, in heartbreaking detail, the *shape* of the silence that follows. A silence heavy as mercy. Hollow as a held breath. I wept. I am not ashamed to tell you. I wept because I know that silence. We all do.

And yet—here is the terrible, shimmering beauty of it—the manuscript does not drown in sorrow. It lets the melancholy in, yes, but it also holds a candle to it. There is a line that runs through several poems like a golden thread: *"Even the dying star remembers how to shine before it goes."* The poet speaks of hope not as something loud and triumphant, but as a quiet, stubborn persistence. Hope as a frayed rope you keep holding. Hope as a window left unlatched, just in case.

I sit here now, torn in two.

Part of me wants to hide this book in the deepest folds of my coat, to press it against my chest and never let another soul see it. It feels like a violation to read it, as if I am spying on a raw, unguarded heart. To share it would be to expose the poet’s deepest wounds to the cold air of strangers. The fear is visceral—what if they mock it? What if they do not understand?

But the other part of me—the part that is writing to you now—is desperate. Desperate for someone else to know that they exist. That these words *matter*. That they are not just the echo of one person’s pain, but a mirror held up to the universal ache. The longing we carry for lives we didn’t live. The desire that burns like a fever even as it consumes us. The melancholy that is not a sickness, but a kind of knowing—a quiet, tender awareness that we are here for such a brief, brilliant, impossible moment.

In reading these verses, I have felt less alone. And that is the most terrifying, beautiful gift a stranger’s words can give.

So I ask you, my friend, who has also wandered through the graveyards of forgotten libraries: Have you ever held a voice that was not your own, yet felt it speak directly from the marrow of your bones? Have you ever bled for a stranger’s heartbreak?

I think I will copy a line or two, tuck them into the lining of my coat, and leave the manuscript exactly where I found it. Let it be a secret between the dust and the angels. But I am writing this to you so that, somewhere, the echo of it lives. So that you know: there are words out there that are waiting to find you, too—that will hold you and break you and, somehow, piece you back together just slightly differently.

Yours, in the beautiful ache of recognition,

A Temporary Custodian of Lost Light
